name: Kaapor
catalog_quote: Three degrees of stress are recognized: heavy stress ["], primary stress ['], and secondary stress [˚]. Heavy stress is significant within the phonological clause and often coincides with emphasis (see 4.32). Primary stress always occurs on the final syllable of words: /tata/ [ta'ta] 'fire'. Secondary stress most commonly occurs on every second syllable counting back from the primary stress in no…

new_statements.quote: A acentuação é predizível, caindo sempre na última sílaba das palavras sem necessidade de ser escrita. Os sufixos levam acentuação primária, o que significa que a acentuação da palavra passa para o sufixo. [§1, PDF p. 2] — Os sufixos são unidos com hífen para identificá-los. Existe para tal prática um motivo fonológico, ou seja o padrão de acentuação. [nota 4, PDF p. 19]
new_statements.translation: Stress is predictable, always falling on the last syllable of words, with no need for it to be written. Suffixes take primary stress, which means that the word's stress moves to the suffix. [§1] — Suffixes are joined with a hyphen to identify them. There is a phonological reason for this practice, namely the stress pattern. [note 4]
new_statements.citation: Kakumasu, James Y. (1976). Gramática gerativa preliminar da língua urubú. Série Lingüística 5. Brasília. pp. 171-197.
new_statements.locator: §1 'Sistematização fonética' (the orthography note), PDF p. 2 of 21; the re-typeset PDF carries no printed page numbers, the printed article runs pp. 171-197 so this is the first or second printed page (≈ p. 171-172). Footnote 4, 'Notas', PDF p. 19.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (21 pp., text layer, Distiller 2006, title 'a-SL-5 Pgs 171-197 Urubu.doc'; the PDF's metadata confirms). extracted text of PDF p. 2, section '1. SISTEMATIZAÇÃO FONÉTICA', reads verbatim: 'A acentuação é predizível, caindo sempre na última sílaba das palavras sem necessidade de ser escrita. Os sufixos levam acentuação primária, o que significa que a acentuação da palavra passa para o sufixo.' PDF p. 19 under 'NOTAS', note 4, reads verbatim: 'Os sufixos são unidos com hífen para identificá-los. Existe para tal prática um motivo fonológico, ou seja o padrão de acentuação.' A a full-text search for stress/accent the whole text layer for acentu/acento/tônic/sílaba/stress finds only these…
new_statements.relation_note: Catalog (StressTyp2) records Kaapor as final primary stress with alternating secondary stress (alternating stress from the right). Kakumasu 1976 states final, fully predictable primary stress that shifts onto suffixes — same placement. It is silent on the secondary alternating stresses the StressTyp2 record encodes, and adds the domain detail that the final suffix carries the stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fully predictable and always falls on the last syllable of the word; when a suffix is added the primary stress moves onto the (final) suffix, so the stress domain is the morphological word including suffixes. Nothing is said about secondary stress, weight, or exceptions.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; 'sempre' (always). The only detail is that suffixes attract primary stress, i.e. stress stays word-final after suffixation; hyphenation of suffixes in the orthography is justified by this stress pattern (note 4).
new_statements.identity_note: Kakumasu calls the language 'Urubu' (= Urubú-Kaapor / Ka'apor), footnote 1: Tupi-Guarani family, about 500 speakers in northeastern Brazil, data collected over ~10 years under SIL; no dialect is distinguished. Same language as the catalog's Kaapor (urub1250).

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-strict' final primary stress with alternating secondary leftward (alternating stress from the right) rests on Kakumasu 1968 §4.1, and the deciding sentence is on the typescript scan we hold at p. 15 exactly as quoted (scanned-verified from the image-only PDF). Suffixed words keep final primary stress (suffix takes it), clitics do not perturb it (pp. 15-16), so the word domain and strictness are consistent with the source. A second, independent, first-hand description (Caldas 2009 UnB dissertation, §2.3 p. 43) was downloaded now and confirms final stress, noting only 'a few words' with penultimate stress — a lexical-exception remark that does not change a fixed: final syllable classification but could be recorded in the 'the exceptions statement'/caution field. Lopes 2009 (held) has no stress section but every stress-marked form is final-stressed. No later phonology or instrumental study appears in Glottolog 5.1 or in Caldas's

sources.quote: "Em Ka'apór observa-se a ocorrência de maior intensidade expiratória na última sílaba da palavra, quando se tem duas ou mais sílabas. Há poucas palavras cuja intensidade expiratória recai na penúltima sílaba." (Word stress = greatest expiratory intensity on the final syllable of words of two or more syllables; a few words have penultimate stress.) All phonemic transcriptions in the chapter mark final stress, e.g. /mo'nok/ 'cortar', /ru'waj/ 'rabo', /tÈapua'pu/ 'trovão'.
